title: Greedy Best-First on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing Greedy Best-First pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — Why it sprints to the goal ⚡ (and when it fails)

In this Barcelona (Eixample) grid demo, each node’s priority is purely: h(n) = heuristic distance to the destination.
✅ Greedy Best-First chooses the next move that *looks* closest.
❌ Unlike A*, it does NOT balance cost-so-far g(n) + h(n), so it can tunnel into dead-ends or “pretty” corridors that lead to longer paths.

What you’ll observe:
• Rapid expansion toward the target (frontier shoots forward)
• Sudden backtracking or detours when obstacles invalidate the greedy guess
• A-star-style behavior would prefer safer routes by accounting for accumulated path cost

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First can be blazingly fast on well-behaved maps, but it’s not guaranteed to find the optimal path.

Debate question: Would you rather have “fast-but-wrong sometimes” or “slower-but-reliably optimal” in real routing?

Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — in Barcelona (Eixample)! ⚡

In this Shorts video, we visualize how greedy best first search expands nodes using ONLY a heuristic pathfinding estimate (h(n)). You’ll compare greedy vs a star behavior: Greedy can look incredibly efficient but may fail to find the shortest route, especially around obstacles.

✅ What you’ll learn:
• heuristic pathfinding (h(n))
• greedy best first search mechanics
• why Greedy Best-First differs from A* (missing g(n) cost)
